start.text:
The nursing handover at bay 4:

'Mrs. Margaret Osei, 78, brought in by her daughter at 09:15. Daughter says Mum has been "not herself" since yesterday morning — confused, not making sense, very drowsy. She lives alone but her daughter visits daily. No falls, no head injury. No complaint of pain. She has hypertension and Type 2 diabetes. Takes several medications.'

You approach the bay. Mrs. Osei is sitting up in bed, looking at the ceiling. She glances at you when you speak but her answers are muddled and she can't tell you what day it is or where she is. She does not appear to be in distress.

Vitals: HR 102 | BP 114/70 | RR 18 | Temp 38.3°C | SpO₂ 97% | GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6)

The daughter is sitting beside her, looking worried.

What is your first priority?

choices.text: Speak to the daughter immediately — collateral history is essential in any confused elderly patient

choices.text: Order an urgent CT head — she could be having a stroke

effects.reason: CT head ordered before any metabolic or infectious workup — premature. Acute confusion in an elderly patient is far more likely to be metabolic or infectious in origin. Stroke is certainly possible but should not be the first test.

collateral-history.text:
Mrs. Osei's daughter, Abena, tells you:

'She's been different since yesterday. She kept asking where Dad was — he died six years ago. Last night she didn't sleep at all, she was calling out and she got up twice not knowing where she was. This morning she couldn't finish a sentence.

She was completely normal four days ago — we had lunch together. I noticed she had been drinking less water because it's been cold. She mentioned her urine smelled strange two days ago but said it was nothing.

Her medications are: Amlodipine 5mg, Metformin 500mg BD, Lisinopril 5mg, and she was given Trimethoprim last month for a water infection but I'm not sure if she finished the course.'

BASELINE: She is sharp and independent normally. This is ACUTE onset over 24–48 hours. She has no prior psychiatric history.

glucose-result.text:
Bedside blood glucose: 6.2 mmol/L (112 mg/dL)

Within normal range. Hypoglycaemia is excluded as a cause of Mrs. Osei's confusion.

This is an important first step — in a diabetic patient on Metformin, hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia can present with acute confusion. Neither is the cause here.

Your differential now needs to account for:
• Infection (she has a fever and reported offensive urine)
• Dehydration / electrolyte disturbance
• Medication effects
• Neurological cause (less likely given acute onset and fever — but not yet excluded)

premature-ct-node.text:
The radiographer takes Mrs. Osei for a CT head. The scan takes 35 minutes.

CT Head Report: No acute intracranial pathology. No haemorrhage. No large infarct. Age-appropriate cortical atrophy. No midline shift.

The scan is NORMAL.

While she was in radiology, the nurse noted a urine sample in the bedpan — concentrated and cloudy with an offensive smell. Temperature has now risen to 38.7°C.

You have spent 35 minutes on a test that was negative. The infectious workup has not yet begun.

The nursing consultant walks past and raises an eyebrow. 'In a febrile 78-year-old with acute confusion — did the CT change your management?'

choices.text: Order urinalysis and bloods — CT was normal, infection now seems most likely

physical-exam.text:
Physical and Neurological Examination:

General: Elderly woman, flushed, mildly diaphoretic. Answers questions inconsistently. Cannot state the date, month, or where she is. Intermittently picks at the bedsheet. Fluctuating attention — she drifts mid-sentence.

Hands: No clubbing, no asterixis (no hepatic/uraemic flap).
Neck: Supple — no neck stiffness, no photophobia (meningitis less likely).
Chest: Clear to auscultation bilaterally. No wheeze or crackles.
Abdomen: Soft. Mild suprapubic tenderness on deep palpation. No guarding. Mild right costovertebral angle tenderness.
Skin: No petechiae or purpuric rash. No jaundice.

Neurological: Cranial nerves grossly intact. No focal motor or sensory deficit. No facial droop. No dysarthria. Arms and legs move symmetrically.

KEY FINDINGS:
• Acute FLUCTUATING confusion — not a fixed deficit
• Suprapubic tenderness and right CVA tenderness
• No focal neurological signs
• Fever

This is a delirium picture with a strong localising clue pointing to a urinary source.

choices.text: This is an acute delirium — the fluctuating confusion, fever, and urinary symptoms together point to a medical cause

effects.reason: Acute delirium correctly identified — not stroke, not baseline dementia. Fluctuating onset, no focal neurology, and fever all point to a reversible medical cause.

choices.text: No focal deficit but I'm concerned about a stroke — I want a CT head

stroke-concern-node.text:
You are concerned about stroke as a cause of Mrs. Osei's confusion.

The ED consultant walks over and reviews your assessment.

'Let's think through this. She has a fever, acute-onset fluctuating confusion, is 78 years old, and her daughter reports she smelled abnormal urine two days ago. There are no focal neurological findings on your exam. No facial droop, no arm weakness, no dysarthria.

Stroke absolutely belongs on the differential. But in an elderly patient with fever, fluctuating confusion, and possible urinary symptoms — what is the far more common cause?'

She's prompting you to think about base rates: delirium secondary to infection is vastly more common than new stroke presenting as isolated confusion without focal deficits.

choices.text: You're right — I'll rule out metabolic and infectious causes first before imaging

effects.reason: Correctly prioritised infectious/metabolic workup over premature neuroimaging after clinical prompting

choices.text: I still want the CT head first — stroke can't wait

delirium-recognised.text:
ACUTE DELIRIUM IDENTIFIED.

Your working differential for the CAUSE:
1. Urinary tract infection / urosepsis — most likely (fever, CVA tenderness, offensive urine reported)
2. Dehydration / electrolyte disturbance — likely contributing
3. Medication side effect — possible (Lisinopril, Metformin; trimethoprim course possibly incomplete)
4. Stroke — possible but no focal signs; less likely without lateralising findings

Delirium is always medical until proven otherwise.

Key teaching: Never attribute acute confusion to 'dementia' or 'baseline' without ruling out a reversible medical cause — especially in a patient whose daughter confirms this is acutely different from normal.

What is your next priority?

choices.text: Order urinalysis, blood glucose, and a blood panel immediately
Review her medications carefully for contributing drug effects

effects.reason: Medications reviewed for contributing causes — important step in elderly confusion workup

medication-review.text:
Medication review with the daughter's input:

• Amlodipine 5mg OD — calcium channel blocker for hypertension. Can occasionally cause peripheral vasodilation and headache. Not a significant cause of delirium.
• Metformin 500mg BD — can rarely cause lactic acidosis but this requires impaired renal function. Not a primary delirium cause at this dose.
• Lisinopril 5mg OD — ACE inhibitor. Well tolerated. Unlikely to cause confusion.
• Trimethoprim (incomplete course) — prescribed last month for urinary tract infection. The daughter is not sure if she completed the course. This is highly significant.

CONCLUSION: No medication is primarily responsible for the delirium, but the incomplete antibiotic course is a red flag. It suggests a previous UTI that may not have been fully treated, with bacterial persistence or resistance now driving urosepsis.

This strongly reinforces UTI as the primary diagnosis.

choices.text: Proceed to investigations — urinalysis and bloods

investigation-hub.text:
What investigations do you want to order for Mrs. Osei?

Current working differential:
1. UTI / urosepsis causing delirium (most likely)
2. Electrolyte disturbance / dehydration
3. Medication effects
4. Stroke (less likely — no focal signs)

Choose wisely — time matters and her temperature is 38.3°C with HR 102.

urinalysis-result.text:
Urinalysis with Microscopy — RESULTED:

Appearance: Cloudy, dark amber, offensive odour
Leukocyte esterase: POSITIVE (++)
Nitrites: POSITIVE
WBC: >50 per high-power field
Red blood cells: 8 per hpf
Bacteria: Many
pH: 6.5 | Protein: Trace

CONCLUSION: This is a highly positive urinalysis with multiple markers of significant urinary tract infection.

[!] Leukocyte esterase and nitrites BOTH positive in a symptomatic patient is highly specific for UTI.
[!] WBC >50/hpf indicates significant pyuria consistent with urosepsis.

This result, in the context of Mrs. Osei's fever (38.3°C), tachycardia (HR 102), and acute confusion, satisfies criteria for UROSEPSIS — a systemic response to urinary tract infection.

You now have your diagnosis.

bloods-result.text:
Blood Results — RESULTED:

CBC:
  WBC: 16.8 ×10⁹/L [↑] (reference 4.0–11.0) — leukocytosis, neutrophil predominance
  Haemoglobin: 11.4 g/dL [↓ mild] — consistent with chronic mild anaemia of age
  Platelets: 198 ×10⁹/L — normal

BMP:
  Na: 131 mmol/L [↓] — mild hyponatraemia (likely dehydration)
  K: 3.9 mmol/L — normal
  Creatinine: 128 μmol/L [↑] — mildly elevated (baseline unknown; possible AKI superimposed)
  Urea: 11.4 mmol/L [↑] — raised, consistent with dehydration
  Glucose: 7.1 mmol/L — mildly elevated, no hypoglycaemia

CRP: 142 mg/L [↑↑] — significantly elevated, strongly suggestive of bacterial infection
Lactate: 2.3 mmol/L [↑ borderline] — borderline elevated; suggests early metabolic stress

Blood cultures: ×2 sets sent — pending 48–72h

SUMMARY: Leukocytosis, elevated CRP, mild AKI, hyponatraemia, and borderline lactate in the context of a highly positive urinalysis confirms UROSEPSIS. Renal function must be considered when choosing antibiotics.

uti-diagnosis.text:
DIAGNOSIS: Urosepsis causing acute delirium.

Mrs. Osei meets sepsis criteria:
• Suspected infection source confirmed (urinalysis positive)
• Acute organ dysfunction: confusion (new), borderline AKI, lactate 2.3 mmol/L

She is haemodynamically borderline — HR 102, BP 114/70. Not yet in shock, but the trend is concerning, especially in an elderly patient with limited physiological reserve.

Her prior trimethoprim course appears to have been incomplete, which may have selected for resistant organisms.

What treatment do you want to initiate?

choices.text: IV co-amoxiclav (or local empirical antibiotic) + IV fluids 500 mL sodium chloride + urine culture sent

effects.reason: Appropriate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics initiated for urosepsis — correct agent and route
IV fluid resuscitation initiated for tachycardia, dehydration, and borderline haemodynamics

choices.text: Oral trimethoprim — she had it before and it worked

effects.reason: Oral trimethoprim is inappropriate for urosepsis: (1) IV route required for reliable bioavailability in a confused patient who may not swallow reliably, (2) prior incomplete trimethoprim course raises concern for resistance

choices.text: Wait for culture results before prescribing antibiotics

effects.reason: Waiting for culture results before treating urosepsis is dangerous — cultures take 48–72 hours and sepsis can progress to shock within hours. Empirical treatment should begin immediately.

She is also confused, which makes reliable oral absorption uncertain. And her HR is 102 with a temperature of 38.3°C — this is urosepsis, not an uncomplicated UTI. IV route is recommended.'

Do you want to revise your antibiotic plan?

delayed-treatment-node.text:
[DETERIORATION] One hour passes. Mrs. Osei has received no IV antibiotics.

The nurse calls urgently: 'Doctor — she is worse. Very drowsy now, only opens her eyes to voice. HR 124, BP 96/58. Temperature 39.1°C. She looks grey.'

She is developing septic shock.

The senior consultant has been called. She walks in, takes one look, and starts issuing orders while looking at you: 'IV access — now. Fluids — now. Broad-spectrum antibiotics — now. What have we been doing for the last hour?'

You have lost critical time.

choices.text: Immediately start IV co-amoxiclav, IV fluids, and arrange HDU admission

effects.reason: IV antibiotics finally started — but septic shock has already developed due to delay

treatment-optimal.text:
IV co-amoxiclav commenced. 500 mL 0.9% NaCl running. Urine culture sent.

Mrs. Osei's observations after 20 minutes: HR 90 (↓ from 102), BP 118/72 (improved). Temperature 38.1°C.

She is starting to make more sense: 'Where is Abena?' — her daughter is right there. She recognises her.

Abena grips her mother's hand. 'Mum — you're back.'

Remaining to do:
• Safe disposition — ward admission (not discharge)
• Consider urine culture results for antibiotic de-escalation after 24–48h
• Recheck renal function in 24h (mild AKI noted)
• Ensure blood cultures resulted
• Safety: falls risk, delirium precautions

What is your disposition decision?

choices.text: Admit to general medical ward — IV antibiotics, monitoring, renal recheck, delirium precautions

effects.reason: Correctly admitted to medical ward — urosepsis in an elderly delirious patient cannot be managed at home

choices.text: She looks better — discharge with oral antibiotics and GP follow-up

effects.reason: Discharging an elderly urosepsis patient who presented with delirium, AKI, and borderline haemodynamics is unsafe — ongoing IV therapy, monitoring, and renal function tracking are required

outcome-excellent.text:
Mrs. Osei is admitted to the general medicine ward on bay 3. IV co-amoxiclav continues for 48 hours. She is kept hydrated with IV fluids until she can tolerate reliable oral intake.

By the following morning: she is sitting up, fully oriented, asking for tea and a biscuit. 'I'm sorry I caused such a fuss,' she tells Abena. 'I must have been confused.'

Abena is crying.

--- Results ---
Urine culture: E. coli sensitive to co-amoxiclav — antibiotic de-escalated to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate at 48h
Renal function (Day 2): Creatinine 101 μmol/L — AKI resolved with hydration
Sodium (Day 2): 137 mmol/L — hyponatraemia corrected
Discharge: Day 3 with 5-day oral antibiotic course and GP letter

[!] Teaching Point: Acute delirium in the elderly is a medical emergency. The most common reversible causes are infection, metabolic disturbance, and medications. Always take collateral history, check glucose first, and never attribute acute confusion to 'baseline dementia' without a full workup.

outcome-complicated.text:
Mrs. Osei is transferred to the High Dependency Unit.

Septic shock is treated aggressively: IV co-amoxiclav, 30 mL/kg fluid resuscitation over 3 hours, vasopressor support initiated as BP continues to fall.

--- Results ---
Blood culture: E. coli — confirmed urosepsis
AKI worsened to Stage 2 — nephrology review requested
ICU: 2 days, HDU: 3 further days
Discharge: Day 8, requiring outpatient renal follow-up

She survives, but with impaired renal function that persists at discharge. The fall into septic shock was entirely preventable.

[!] Teaching Point: One hour of delay in antibiotic therapy for sepsis is associated with a measurable increase in mortality and organ dysfunction. In an elderly patient with limited reserve, urosepsis escalates rapidly. Empirical treatment should not wait for culture results.

outcome-discharge-error.text:
Mrs. Osei is discharged with a prescription for oral trimethoprim.

14 hours later, Abena calls an ambulance. Her mother is unresponsive on the kitchen floor.

She is brought back to the ED in septic shock: BP 72/40, HR 136, GCS 9. She is intubated and transferred to ICU.

Blood culture: E. coli — trimethoprim resistant (predicated by the incomplete prior course).

--- Results ---
ICU: 9 days, intubated
Post-ICU: Severe functional decline
Discharge: care facility required; independent living no longer possible
Renal function: chronic AKI — remains on fluid restriction

She survives, but the woman who walked into the ED today will not walk out of hospital.

[!] Teaching Point: An elderly patient with urosepsis, AKI, delirium, and tachycardia is NEVER safe for discharge. Clinical improvement after IV fluids and initial antibiotics is not cure — it is stabilisation. Discharge must never be the easy option.
